I'm approaching this challenge with an open mind, a willingness to learn and the ambition to push beyond what I already know. Always excited to explore the intersection of technology.
summary:
NASA missions have gathered terabytes of Martian surface telemetry, yet this critical data remains scattered across disparate archives. During an astronaut Extravehicular Activity (EVA) or rover sortie, navigating without paved roads, physical landmarks, or GPS requires real-time terrain intelligence to prevent fatal cliff falls, rover rollover, or wheel entrapment in soft sand.

ARES is an autonomous tactical decision-support and traverse-planning platform for Martian surface exploration. ARES unifies NASA Mars Trek imagery, MOLA laser altimetry, Curiosity MSL in-situ radiation records, and the official USGS Gazetteer of 2,055 planetary landmarks into an interactive, high-performance geospatial engine. 

Using an terrain-cost A* pathfinding algorithm, ARES dynamically navigates around impassable scarps and active sand dunes, computing optimized corridors for Safest, Shortest, and Science-Focused sorties. Each route is evaluated against NASA spacesuit biomechanical constraints—simulating metabolic calorie burn, oxygen duration, and wheel traction limits in Mars’s 0.38g gravity to ensure astronaut survival.
details:
ARES is an autonomous navigation and decision-support platform for Martian surface exploration:

  • Interactive Mars GIS: Combines a 3D Planetary Globe (ArcGIS) with a sub-meter 2D Tactical Map (OpenLayers) displaying NASA Mars Trek imagery and MOLA elevation.
  • AI Terrain Pathfinding: Uses an A* algorithm calibrated to 0.38g gravity to navigate around steep cliffs and sand dunes, generating Safest, Shortest, and Science-Focused routes.
  • Life-Support Diagnostics: Automatically calculates astronaut calorie burn, oxygen duration, slope rollover risk, and travel time to assign each route a safety grade.

What benefits does it have and what is its intended impact?

  • Astronaut Survival: Prevents fatal falls and vehicle wheel-entrapment in treacherous sand traps like the Bagnold Dunes.
  • On-Site Autonomy: Overcomes the 4 to 24-minute communication delay with Earth by giving crews instant, local route planning without waiting for Mission Control.
  • Unified NASA Data: Transforms fragmented orbital telemetry into actionable surface navigation corridors.

What tools and software did you use?

  • Frontend: React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Lucide Icons, and Framer Motion.
  • Mapping Engines: OpenLayers 10 (2D Tactical Map) and ArcGIS Maps SDK for JavaScript (3D Planetary SceneView).
  • Backend & Data: Node.js, SQLite with R-Tree spatial indexing, PostGIS migration scripts, and Vercel Serverless Functions.
  • Algorithms: Priority-queue A* pathfinding, spherical Martian distance math, and dynamic spatial clustering.

How is your project creative?

  • 0.38g Gravity Bioenergetics: Rather than using flat Euclidean distance, pathfinding incorporates NASA metabolic models—penalizing steep uphill climbs where spacesuit oxygen consumption spikes.
  • Living Telemetry: Integrates real Curiosity rover surface telemetry (Gale Crater pressure, temperatures, dust opacity) and space weather radiation alerts.
  • Dynamic USGS Gazetteer: Queries over 2,055 official USGS planetary landmarks in under 1 millisecond with antimeridian crossing support.
  • Physical Martian Limits: Rover wheel-slip thresholds (18°), spacesuit walking limits (22°), diurnal temperature swings (-12°C to -82°C), and cosmic radiation exposure.
  • Zero-Failure Architecture: Engineered with a dual-layer system (serverless APIs with static CDN GeoJSON fallback) ensuring uninterrupted operation even in offline or bandwidth-limited environments.
